name: JFE2140DR
title: Matched dual N-channel JFET, ultra-low noise and low gate current, for audio front ends
summary: Two N-channel junction FETs in one package, matched to within 4 mV of each other in gate-to-source voltage at 2 mA, for low-noise, very high impedance input stages such as microphone, hydrophone and piezo preamplifiers. Input voltage noise is 1.1 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz with 2 mA drain current (0.9 nV/√Hz at 5 mA), gate current is 10 pA at most at 25 °C and input resistance is about 1 TΩ. Each gate, drain and source has an internal diode to two clamp pins, VCH and VCL, which can be left open. Drain-to-source breakdown is at least 40 V; the part comes in an 8-pin SOIC and a 2 mm × 2 mm 8-pin WSON and is specified from -40 °C to +125 °C.

circuits.title: AC and noise measurement circuit
circuits.description: One JFET runs common-source with a 10 kΩ drain load from V+ and a 10 kΩ source resistor to V-, the source bypassed to ground by 3 mF; the gate is driven from VIN through 0 Ω. The drain signal is ac-coupled by 1 µF into an OPA210 wired as a non-inverting amplifier (10 kΩ over 100 Ω, a 100 kΩ bias resistor at its input) with a 49.9 Ω output resistor. V- is trimmed to set IDS, then V+ to set VDS; the VIN-to-VOUT gain is measured and used to refer the output noise to the input.
notes: One channel of the pair is used.

circuits.title: Clamp diodes protecting a phantom-powered microphone input
circuits.description: A 48 V phantom supply feeds the microphone line through 6.8 kΩ, and a 10 µF capacitor CDC blocks that dc from the gate. If the line is shorted to ground (the switch) while CDC is charged, CDC drives the gate far negative; the internal diode from the gate to VCL conducts and the current iG flows through RG and RL instead, which keeps VGS inside its rating. RB biases the gate to ground. VCH is left open. RG should stay small because its thermal noise adds directly at the gate.
notes: One channel of the pair is used.

circuits.title: Cascode connection of the two JFETs
circuits.description: The lower JFET is the input device, its gate at VIN and its source to ground through RS. The upper JFET sits in series in its drain, gate held at VBIAS, and the output is taken across RD from VDD. The cascode raises the output impedance and so the gain, and holds the input device at low VDS, which keeps its gate current low. VBIAS must be high enough that both JFETs stay saturated; the upper device may also be another kind of transistor.
notes: JFET 1 is the input device and JFET 2 the cascode device.

circuits.title: Common-source amplifier
circuits.description: An open-loop gain stage: VIN drives the gate through RG, RS from source to ground sets the bias current with the JFET threshold, and the output is the drain, loaded by RD from V+. The gain is -gm·RD / (1 + gm·RS); more bias current raises gm, so more gain and lower input-referred noise.
notes: One channel of the pair is used.

circuits.title: Common-source amplifier with a current-source bias
circuits.description: The source resistor of the common-source stage is replaced by a current sink IBIAS to V-, with CS from the source to ground. The bias current no longer depends on the JFET threshold, and since the sink has a high output impedance a smaller CS gives the same filtering.
notes: One channel of the pair is used; IBIAS pin 1 is where the current enters.

circuits.title: Voltage-feedback composite amplifier
circuits.description: The pair is a differential input stage in front of an op amp. Each drain has a load RD from VDD and feeds one op-amp input (JFET 1 to the inverting input, JFET 2 to the non-inverting input). The sources meet through two degeneration resistors RS1 at a node that returns to ground through RS2 bypassed by CS2. VIN drives gate 1 through RG; gate 2 is the feedback node, RF1 from VOUT and RF2 to ground, so the closed-loop gain is 1 + RF1/RF2 while the JFETs give the low noise and high input impedance.

circuits.title: Low-noise, low-power composite amplifier on a 9 V battery
circuits.description: A single-ended audio preamplifier for battery equipment. The JFET pair, loaded by 2.49 kΩ drain resistors from +4.5 V, drives one half of an OPA1692; the sources meet through two 49.9 Ω resistors and the tail goes to ground through 499 Ω bypassed by 100 nF. The input has a 1 MΩ bias resistor to ground and 10 Ω in series with gate 1. Gate 2 is the feedback node, with 100 Ω to ground; the path to VOUT runs through RF3 (10 kΩ rheostat, GAIN), RF2 (499 Ω) and RF1 (10 kΩ rheostat, BASS BOOST, bypassed by 10 nF), with 100 pF across the whole path. Being dc coupled through the pair, the stage reaches low frequencies without large blocking capacitors. The other OPA1692 half splits the 9 V battery: it buffers the midpoint of a 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider (0.1 µF across each half), with 0.1 µF from its output to its inverting input and 10 kΩ from that input to the ground node, which it drives through 100 Ω; the ground node is decoupled by 0.1 µF to each rail.

circuits.title: High input impedance differential front end for an OPA1637
circuits.description: A balanced microphone input on an XLR connector: pin 1 drives gate 1 and pin 2 drives gate 2, each through 10 Ω, and pin 3 is grounded. The matched pair, with 1.5 kΩ drain loads from +5 V and two 49.9 Ω resistors joining the sources, takes the place of the resistor matching a fully differential amplifier would need, so CMRR stays high and the input impedance stays very high. The tail current comes from an N-channel MOSFET held by an OPA197: the op amp forces the voltage of a 10 kΩ / 20 Ω divider between the rails across the 10 Ω source resistor. The drains feed an OPA1637 through 2 kΩ input resistors, with 2 kΩ feedback taken after the 20 Ω output resistors and 1 nF across each feedback path; 100 Ω and 47 pF / 1 nF / 47 pF filter the outputs into the ADC.
notes: The OPA1637 power-down pin goes to 5 V.
CA1 and CA3 return to the ADC ground, GND_ADC, kept apart from the input ground.

operation.text: A matched pair of N-channel JFETs on a precision analog bipolar process, aimed at low-noise gain stages for sensors and microphones with very high output impedance: piezo sensors, transducers, large condenser capsules, hydrophones. It has a high gm to CISS ratio and very low gate current, and input protection diodes are built in.
The quiescent drain current is set by the surrounding circuit anywhere from 50 µA to 20 mA. At 5 mA the input voltage noise is 0.9 nV/√Hz.

Mismatch between the two input devices of a differential pair costs gain accuracy and common-mode rejection, and where a composite amplifier has high dc gain it shows up as offset. The two JFETs are tested to ±4 mV VGS matching; the spread of a production lot is in the mismatch histogram.

Noise falls into a flicker (1/f) region, important for gain below about 100 Hz, and a wideband thermal region above about 1 kHz. Thermal noise depends on gm and so on the drain bias current: more current, less noise. Input current noise is shot noise of the gate current; with gate current this low it is negligible next to the thermal noise of the source impedance in almost every case (noise contributors curve).
Gate current is 10 pA at most at room temperature. As in any JFET it rises with drain-to-source voltage; the lowest gate current comes with VDS below 5 V.

Diodes run from the gate, source and drain of each JFET to two clamp pins, VCL and VCH. When a gate, source or drain goes below VCL or above VCH, current is steered into that pin. The diodes take surges of 200 mA for 50 ms; continuous current should stay under 20 mA. Their leakage is very low, so no external clamps with high leakage or nonlinear capacitance are needed. They are optional: VGS withstands -40 V, and VCL and VCH are left open when the clamps are not used.

Phantom power usually supplies 48 V through 6.8 kΩ. With the microphone unplugged the dc blocking capacitor can charge to 48 V; shorting its input to ground then pushes the gate past its VGS rating unless the clamp diode, with current limited by RG and RL, holds it. RG should be kept low because its thermal noise appears directly at the gate.

It behaves as a standard N-channel depletion JFET. Below VGSC the channel is off and only junction leakage flows. Above VGSC, at low VDS the device is in the linear region and acts as a drain-to-source resistor that VGS hardly changes; above the saturation threshold IDS depends strongly on VGS, through gm.

The pair works as a differential stage inside the feedback loop, which gives gain down to low frequencies with no large dc-blocking capacitors. Choose the bias current from the trade-off between noise and current (noise against drain current curve) and set it with the source resistance (IDS against RS curve). Then make the drain resistors as large as possible while keeping at least 1 V from drain to source, so the JFETs stay out of the linear region. RF1, RF2 and RF3 set the overall gain; CF3 may be needed for stability depending on the gain setting, which should be checked at both ends of the range.

Stacking another transistor on top of the input device raises the output impedance and the gain, and shields the input node from the gate current that grows at higher VDS. VBIAS must keep both devices saturated. The cascode device need not be a JFET.

With a source resistor, IDS follows RS and the threshold voltage (equal to VGSC), so it varies with both tolerances, and the thermal noise of RS enters the gain. A current-source bias removes the threshold variation and, because a current source has a high output impedance, needs a smaller bypass capacitor CS for the same filtering.

Open-loop JFET stages vary in gain with the forward transconductance. Putting the pair in front of an op amp fixes the gain by resistors, adds open-loop gain and bandwidth beyond the op amp alone, and gives an ultra-low noise, high impedance input for high-impedance microphones.

In ordinary difference or fully differential amplifiers the resistor tolerances set the CMRR, and their input resistors rule out high input impedance. The matched pair in front of an FDA removes the need for resistors matched to better than 1 %, and the high input impedance makes CMRR far less sensitive to unequal source impedances.
The part has no supply pins. In systems with supplies of 40 V or more, keep every pin inside its absolute maximum voltage.

Route the input traces far from supply and output traces, crossing noisy traces at right angles where they must cross. Keep input traces short; they are the most sensitive nodes. Keep high-impedance inputs away from noisy traces, filter the supplies well, and place the source and drain components close to the part. A guard ring round the gate traces, driven from a low impedance, reduces leakage from nearby traces at other potentials. Clean the board after assembly.
Moisture absorbed into the plastic package can shift a precision part. After aqueous cleaning, bake the assembly; 30 minutes at 85 °C is usually enough.

The exposed pad of the DSG package is soldered to the board, for heat and for mechanical strength. The land pattern allows two optional 0.2 mm vias in the pad; vias under paste should be filled, plugged or tented.
